hook: Before building custom tools, know the powers models bring in the box: **code execution, live web access, computer use, file systems** — each a superpower with a sharp edge.

scenes.title: Let the model write code; **never let it run free**
scenes.narration: The most transformative built-in capability: the model writes code — Python, usually — and a sandbox executes it and returns stdout. Suddenly the model can compute precisely instead of approximating: statistics over a CSV, plots, file conversions, anything code does better than language. This is the pattern behind data-analysis assistants and the code-interpreter mode you met in GA-19. The non-negotiable: the sandbox. Model-generated code is arbitrary code — it can read secrets, delete files, exfiltrate data over the network. Production sandboxes: no network access, a read-only allow-listed file area, CPU and memory limits, a timeout, and an ephemeral filesystem that dies with the session. Treat generated code as hostile; the sandbox is the moat.

items.s: No network · allow-listed read paths · CPU/mem/time limits · ephemeral disk
pandas, NumPy, matplotlib ready → model writes analysis, not plumbing
stdout + artifacts (charts, files) return as observations the model can describe

scenes.narration: Why this capability changes agent design: precision tasks leave the language domain entirely — 'average revenue by quarter, plotted' is a five-line pandas script, not a paragraph of reasoning where arithmetic drifts. The loop becomes: model writes code → sandbox runs → model reads stdout and decides next step — AG-01's loop with execution as the tool. Mature setups add: artifact handling — generated charts and files stored and linkable; a persistent working directory per conversation so multi-step analysis accumulates state; and output truncation discipline — ten thousand rows of stdout is a context bomb, so summarize in-code and return aggregates. Sandboxed code execution is the highest-leverage built-in — and the most dangerous without the sandbox.

scenes.title: The model's training data ends; **the web doesn't**
scenes.sub: Search and fetch as built-in tools
scenes.narration: Two complementary tools. Web search: a query goes to a search API — results return as titles, snippets and URLs; the model reads the landscape and picks what to open. Fetch: a URL is retrieved and converted to clean text — HTML stripped to readable content — and returned as an observation. Together they close the freshness gap from GA-13: stock prices, today's documentation, this week's breaking change, all reachable at query time. The engineering realities: fetch needs care — paywalls, JavaScript-heavy pages, cookie walls and bot detection return garbage; prefer pages with clean markup and provide the model error signals like AG-02 taught. Rate limits apply to your search API. And robots and terms-of-service are legal constraints, not technical ones.

layers.s: Landscape scan · snippets + URLs · the model picks candidates
Clean-text extraction · paywalls/JS = noise → actionable errors back
"As of <date>, …" · sources cited · stale pages flagged by the model

scenes.narration: The research loop this enables: search broadly, fetch the three most promising, synthesize with explicit as-of dates and source links. Two quality disciplines. Source triage: the model should weigh source authority — official documentation beats a random blog — and cross-check single-source claims, because the web confidently repeats itself; one original error becomes fifty copies. Freshness labeling: always state the as-of date in answers built from web data; 'as of October 2026' protects the answer from silently aging. Cost note: search-plus-fetch chains consume tokens fast — fetched pages enter the context window, so truncate aggressively — summary-first, full text only when the summary warrants it. Built-in web tools make agents current; discipline makes them trustworthy.

scenes.title: The last UI: **the model operates a computer**
scenes.sub: Screenshots in, clicks and keys out
scenes.narration: The frontier capability: computer use — the agent receives screenshots and emits low-level actions: click at coordinates, type text, press keys, scroll. Same idea one level up as browser use — drive a web page's DOM: navigate, fill forms, click buttons, read results. Why this matters: it automates systems that have NO API — legacy admin panels, third-party dashboards, internal tools built in 2010. The model perceives the screen visually, plans the next action, acts, screenshots again — AG-01's loop with pixels as observations. The honest caveats: it's slow — seconds per action, so a thirty-step task takes minutes; brittle — a redesigned button or an unexpected popup derails it; and risky — it's literally operating a logged-in session with your credentials.

items.s: Legacy panels, third-party UIs · the API-less integration path of last (and sometimes only) resort
Seconds per action · UI changes break flows · expect retries and confirmation loops
Dedicated accounts · least privilege · human confirmation before irreversible actions

scenes.narration: The decision ladder: prefer a real API, then an MCP server or tool, then structured automation — and only then computer use, because per-action cost and fragility are an order of magnitude worse. When you do deploy it, the safety pattern mirrors AG-02: a dedicated low-privilege account — the agent should never hold YOUR admin session; scoped scope — read-only browsing flows freely, purchases and deletions require human confirmation; and step budgets with screenshots logged for audit. Browser-use variants that drive the DOM are faster and less brittle than pixel-clicking, but share the brittleness — a CSS class rename is a broken tool. Computer use is a genuine superpower for the long tail of un-API-able software — wield it with the respect its power demands.

scenes.title: Files as the agent's workspace — **with guardrails bolted on**
scenes.sub: Read/write tools and the path-scoping rule
scenes.narration: File system tools — list, read, write, append — turn an agent from a talker into a worker that produces artifacts: reports, cleaned datasets, generated code, project scaffolding. The workspace pattern: give the agent a DEDICATED working directory; every read and write resolves against it; paths that escape it — dot-dot tricks, absolute paths outside the root — are rejected. That's the whole security story, and it's non-negotiable: an agent with unrestricted write access and a confused moment is a data-loss incident. Add: extension allow-lists for writes — .md, .csv, .py in the workspace — and size caps on reads so a 'read this file' call can't context-bomb the loop with a gigabyte log.

scenes.title: Path-scoped file tools (the guardrails are the code)
annot: resolve() + prefix check defeats ../ escapes — the one check that makes file tools safe
Read caps turn 'oops read the 2GB log' from a context bomb into an actionable error
Write allow-lists limit blast radius even when the agent is confidently wrong
scenes.narration: Fifty lines, and every safety property of the file tool lives in _safe: resolve the candidate path to its absolute form, then verify it's still inside the workspace — this single prefix check defeats dot-dot escapes, symlinks and absolute-path tricks in one move. The size cap converts a context disaster into an AG-02-style actionable error: 'ask for a specific section'. The write allow-list means even a fully convinced, completely wrong agent can only create markdown, CSVs and Python in a sandbox directory. Compose these with sandboxed code execution from chapter one and the agent gains a full workshop — write code, run it in the sandbox, read results, iterate — the workspace pattern underlying every serious agentic coding and analysis product.

scenes.title: Agent powers assembled. Now aim them at a classic target: databases.
scenes.next: Reel 44 · Text-to-SQL — question in, safe SQL out

recap: Sandboxed code execution gives agents precision — no network, allow-listed reads, resource limits, ephemeral disk
Search + fetch close the freshness gap; synthesize with as-of dates and source triage
Computer/browser use is the no-API last resort — slow, brittle, and guarded by dedicated accounts + human confirmation; file tools live behind path-scoping

quiz.q: What defines a safe code-execution sandbox for agents?
opts: No network access, allow-listed read paths, CPU/memory/time limits, ephemeral storage
quiz.why: Model-generated code is arbitrary code; only environmental isolation makes executing it acceptable.

quiz.q: Why must synthesized web answers carry 'as of' dates?
opts: Web content changes — a dated claim ages visibly; an undated one silently becomes wrong
quiz.why: Freshness is the whole point of web access; dates keep that freshness legible to the reader.

quiz.q: What is the key defensive check in path-scoped file tools?
opts: resolve() the path and verify it's inside the workspace — defeats ../ escapes, symlinks and absolute paths
quiz.why: Canonicalization plus a prefix check is the single guard that makes arbitrary read/write paths safe.

code.title: Capability stack: what to enable, in order of caution
code.body:
# Enable in this order — each step adds power AND guardrail work:

# 1 · SANDBOXED CODE EXECUTION   (start here)
#    e2b / daytona / local container
#    no-net, read-only mounts, 30s timeout, 512MB RAM

# 2 · FILE TOOLS on a workspace  (add when artifacts matter)
#    path-scope (slide 4), ext allow-list, size caps

# 3 · WEB SEARCH + FETCH         (add for freshness)
#    search API w/ quota · fetch w/ truncation + ToS care

# 4 · BROWSER/COMPUTER USE       (last resort, most guarded)
#    dedicated account · human-confirm irreversibles · step budgets

# Anti-pattern: enabling 2-4 BEFORE 1's sandbox exists.
# Generated code + unrestricted files = exfiltration path.
annot: The order is a risk ladder: execution sandbox first because everything else composes with it
Each capability ships with its own guardrail checklist — power without the checklist is an incident report
Audit log every action across all four: built-in capabilities touch the outside world

notes:
# Built-in Capabilities

## Code execution sandbox
- Model writes code → sandbox runs → stdout/artifacts as observations.
- Sandbox: no network, allow-listed reads, CPU/mem/time limits, ephemeral disk.
- Working dir per session; truncate outputs; artifacts stored + linkable.

## Web search & fetch
- search: landscape; fetch: clean-text page → observation.
- Discipline: source triage, as-of dates, truncation (summary-first), ToS.

## Computer / browser use
- For systems with NO API. Screenshots→actions (computer) or DOM (browser).
- Slow, brittle; dedicated accounts, least privilege, human-confirm irreversibles.

## File system tools
- Workspace pattern: resolve()+prefix check, ext allow-list, read caps.
- Composes with sandbox → full agent workshop (write/run/read/iterate).
